items.en: There is milk in the fridge.
There is no bread at home.
Is there a good restaurant here?

lessons.title: I Want To, I Can, I Need To

items.en: Can you help me? (to a man)
They want to see a film.
The little children are in the kindergarten.
My dad is at the hospital.
I am drinking a glass of water. (woman)
I am writing her a letter.
I want to talk with you. (to a man)
This present is for you. (to a man)
Yesterday I was at the sea.
We were in Jerusalem in the summer.
Did you see the new film? (to a man)
What did you do on Shabbat? (to a woman)
I went to the market in the morning.
We went to Haifa by train.
When did you come home? (to a man)
We came to Israel a year ago.
He went to work by bike.
Did you go to the film yesterday? (to a woman)
Tomorrow I'm going to buy a bike.
She is going to study at the university.
We are going to eat at a restaurant.
What are you going to do? (to a woman)
They are going to see grandma.
Next week I'm going to work.
Afterwards we are going to rest.
There are thirty students in the class.
There are a hundred pages in the book.
The bus leaves at half past two.
The shop is closed until ten.
Could I have the menu, please?
Can I have a salad without onion?
I go to work by bus.
The train to Jerusalem is fast.
How do you get to the beach?
The airport is far from the city.
He is an engineer at a big company.
What do you do for work? (to a man)
My brother is taller than me.
This is the most beautiful house on the street.
The train is faster than the bus.
She is the best student in the class.

lessons.title: Reading: A Day in Tel Aviv
lessons.context: Yoni describes a Friday in Tel Aviv.

paragraphs.he: בְּיוֹם שִׁשִּׁי נָסַעְתִּי לְתֵל אָבִיב בְּרַכֶּבֶת.
paragraphs.en: On Friday I went to Tel Aviv by train.
In the morning I went to the market and bought fruit.

paragraphs.he: אַחַר כָּךְ יָשַׁבְתִּי בְּבֵית קָפֶה וְשָׁתִיתִי הָפוּךְ.
paragraphs.en: Then I sat in a café and drank a latte.
At noon I went to the beach with a friend.

paragraphs.he: הַמַּיִם הָיוּ חַמִּים וְהָיָה הַרְבֵּה אֲנָשִׁים.
paragraphs.en: The water was warm and there were a lot of people.

paragraphs.he: בָּעֶרֶב חָזַרְתִּי הַבַּיְתָה עָיֵף אֲבָל שָׂמֵחַ.
paragraphs.en: In the evening I came home tired but happy.

questions.question: How did Yoni get to Tel Aviv?
What did he buy at the market?
What did he drink at the café?
How did he feel in the evening?

a1-yesh-ein.title: There Is and There Isn't: יֵשׁ / אֵין
a1-yesh-ein.pattern: יֵשׁ + noun = there is · אֵין + noun = there isn't · יֵשׁ לִי = I have
a1-yesh-ein.explanation: יֵשׁ means 'there is / there are' and אֵין means 'there isn't / there aren't'. They never change for gender or number. Add לְ + a person to talk about having: יֵשׁ לִי ('I have', literally 'there is to me'), אֵין לָנוּ ('we don't have'). Hebrew has no verb 'to have' at all.
a1-yesh-ein.fact: Because יֵשׁ לִי literally means 'there is to me', Hebrew speakers sometimes say 'there is to me a question' when they speak English.

dialogue.en: No, I don't have time now.

a1-infinitive.title: Want To, Can, Need To
a1-infinitive.explanation: After רוֹצֶה (want), יָכוֹל (can) and צָרִיךְ (need, have to), the next verb is in the infinitive, which starts with לְ or לִ: לִלְמֹד (to study), לֶאֱכֹל (to eat), לָלֶכֶת (to go). The first verb agrees with the speaker: a man says אֲנִי רוֹצֶה, a woman says אֲנִי רוֹצָה; plural רוֹצִים / רוֹצוֹת.
a1-infinitive.fact: אֶפְשָׁר ('it's possible') is the polite all-purpose way to ask for something: אֶפְשָׁר מַיִם? = 'Could I have some water?'

dialogue.native: כֵּן, אֲבָל קֹדֶם אֲנִי צָרִיךְ לַעֲבֹד.
dialogue.en: Yes, but first I need to work.

a1-et.title: The Object Marker אֶת
a1-et.pattern: verb + אֶת + definite noun: אֲנִי רוֹאֶה אֶת הַיֶּלֶד
a1-et.explanation: When the direct object is definite (it has הַ 'the', or it is a name), Hebrew puts the little word אֶת before it: אֲנִי רוֹאֶה אֶת הַבַּיִת ('I see the house'), אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אֶת דָּנָה ('I love Dana'). With an indefinite object there is no אֶת: אֲנִי רוֹאֶה בַּיִת ('I see a house'). אֶת has no translation; it only marks 'this is the object'.
a1-et.fact: אֶת can take endings too: אוֹתִי (me), אוֹתְךָ (you), אוֹתוֹ (him), אוֹתָהּ (her).

a1-def-adj.title: The Big House: הַ on the Adjective Too
a1-def-adj.pattern: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל = the big house · הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל = the house is big
a1-def-adj.explanation: The adjective comes after the noun. When the noun has 'the' (הַ), the adjective gets הַ too: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל ('the big house'). Without the second הַ, it becomes a full sentence: הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל ('the house is big'). Adjectives also agree in gender and number: יֶלֶד קָטָן, יַלְדָּה קְטַנָּה, יְלָדִים קְטַנִּים.
a1-def-adj.fact: This tiny הַ is the whole difference between a phrase and a sentence, because Hebrew has no 'is' in the present tense.

dialogue.en: The new book is on the table.

a1-smichut.title: Word Pairs: Smichut
a1-smichut.pattern: בַּיִת + סֵפֶר → בֵּית סֵפֶר (school, 'house of book')
a1-smichut.explanation: Hebrew joins two nouns into one idea by putting them side by side: the first noun 'belongs to' the second. בֵּית סֵפֶר ('house of book') is a school, חֲדַר שֵׁנָה ('room of sleep') is a bedroom. The first noun often changes its vowels (בַּיִת → בֵּית, חֶדֶר → חֲדַר), and 'the' goes only on the second: בֵּית הַסֵּפֶר ('the school').
a1-smichut.fact: Many everyday words are smichut pairs: בֵּית חוֹלִים (hospital, 'house of the sick'), כַּדּוּרֶגֶל (football, 'ball-foot', written as one word).

a1-li-iti.title: To Me, With Me: Endings on Prepositions
a1-li-iti.pattern: לִי לְךָ לָךְ לוֹ לָהּ · אִתִּי אִתְּךָ אִתּוֹ
a1-li-iti.explanation: Small words like לְ (to), עִם (with) and שֶׁל (of) take person endings instead of a separate pronoun: לִי (to me), לְךָ (to you, m), לָךְ (to you, f), לוֹ (to him), לָהּ (to her), לָנוּ (to us), לָהֶם (to them). 'With' uses the stem אִת־: אִתִּי (with me), אִתְּךָ (with you), אִתּוֹ (with him), אִתָּנוּ (with us).
a1-li-iti.fact: The same endings appear on שֶׁל: שֶׁלִּי (mine), שֶׁלְּךָ (yours), שֶׁלּוֹ (his), so once you know one set you know them all.

a1-haya.title: Was and Had: הָיָה, הָיָה לִי
a1-haya.pattern: הָיִיתִי · הָיִיתָ · הָיָה · הָיְתָה · הָיִינוּ · הָיוּ
a1-haya.explanation: The present tense has no 'is', but the past does: הָיָה (he/it was), הָיְתָה (she/it was), הָיִיתִי (I was), הָיִינוּ (we were), הָיוּ (they were). 'I had' is the past of יֵשׁ לִי: הָיָה לִי (with a masculine thing) or הָיְתָה לִי (with a feminine thing).
a1-haya.fact: אֶתְמוֹל means 'yesterday' and שִׁלְשׁוֹם means 'the day before yesterday'.

dialogue.en: I was at home. I had a fever.

a1-past.title: The Past Tense
a1-past.pattern: כָּתַבְתִּי · כָּתַבְתָּ · כָּתַב · כָּתְבָה · כָּתַבְנוּ · כָּתְבוּ
a1-past.explanation: The past tense is built with endings on the root: -תִּי (I), -תָּ (you, m), -תְּ (you, f), nothing (he), -ָה (she), -נוּ (we), -וּ (they). From כ־ת־ב (write): כָּתַבְתִּי (I wrote), כָּתַב (he wrote), כָּתְבָה (she wrote), כָּתַבְנוּ (we wrote). Because the ending shows the person, the pronoun is often dropped: אָכַלְתִּי = 'I ate'.
a1-past.fact: In the past tense, 'I' and 'we' endings are the same for men and women: a woman also says כָּתַבְתִּי.

dialogue.en: I studied and then I watched a film.

a1-went.title: Went and Came
a1-went.pattern: הָלַכְתִּי (I went) · בָּאתִי (I came) · נָסַעְתִּי (I travelled)
a1-went.explanation: Hebrew distinguishes going on foot from travelling by vehicle: הָלַכְתִּי ('I went, walked') vs נָסַעְתִּי ('I went, drove, travelled'). 'Came' is בָּא: בָּאתִי (I came), הוּא בָּא (he came), הִיא בָּאָה (she came), בָּאנוּ (we came). Notice that בָּא is both 'came' and 'comes': context or a time word decides.
a1-went.fact: When Israelis say they 'went' to another city, they almost always use נָסַע, since nobody walks from Tel Aviv to Haifa.

dialogue.en: How did you get to Eilat?

a1-going-to.title: I'm Going To…
a1-going-to.explanation: Just like English, Hebrew can talk about plans with 'going to': אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ לִקְנוֹת ('I'm going to buy'), הִיא הוֹלֶכֶת לִלְמֹד ('she's going to study'). Use the present tense of הוֹלֵךְ (agreeing with the speaker) + an infinitive. Time words: מָחָר (tomorrow), בַּשָּׁבוּעַ הַבָּא (next week), אַחַר כָּךְ (later).
a1-going-to.fact: Hebrew also has a real future tense (אֶקְנֶה = 'I will buy'), which you'll meet at the next level; 'going to' is the easy way in.

dialogue.en: What are you going to do tomorrow?

a1-numbers.title: Numbers to 100 and Prices
a1-numbers.explanation: Tens end in -ִים: עֶשְׂרִים (20), שְׁלוֹשִׁים (30), אַרְבָּעִים (40), חֲמִשִּׁים (50), שִׁשִּׁים (60), שִׁבְעִים (70), שְׁמוֹנִים (80), תִּשְׁעִים (90), מֵאָה (100). Join units with וְ: עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת (21). Prices are counted in shekels (שֶׁקֶל, plural שְׁקָלִים), and people use the feminine number forms: חֲמִשָּׁה שְׁקָלִים but עֶשְׂרִים שֶׁקֶל in speech. Ask כַּמָּה זֶה עוֹלֶה? ('how much does it cost?').
a1-numbers.fact: The Israeli shekel is often written ₪, and since 1985 it has been the 'new shekel', שֶׁקֶל חָדָשׁ.

a1-time.title: Telling the Time
a1-time.pattern: מָה הַשָּׁעָה? · הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ · בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁבַע
a1-time.explanation: Ask מָה הַשָּׁעָה? ('what's the time?'). Hours use the feminine numbers: הַשָּׁעָה אַחַת (one o'clock), הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ (three o'clock). 'At' a time is בְּשָׁעָה: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁבַע ('at seven'). Half past is וְחֵצִי: שְׁתַּיִם וְחֵצִי (half past two), and a quarter past is וְרֶבַע.
a1-time.fact: In Israel the working week runs Sunday to Thursday; Friday is a short day and Saturday (Shabbat) is the weekend.

a1-cafe.title: At the Café
a1-cafe.explanation: Ordering is easy with אֶפְשָׁר ('is it possible'): אֶפְשָׁר קָפֶה? ('Can I have a coffee?'). Or say אֲנִי רוֹצֶה / רוֹצָה + the item. The bill is הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן. A very Israeli coffee order is הָפוּךְ ('upside down'), a milky coffee like a latte.
a1-cafe.fact: Israeli breakfast in a café usually comes with eggs, a chopped salad, bread, cheeses and dips, and many cafés serve it all day.

dialogue.en: A large latte and water, please.

a1-transport.title: Getting Around
a1-transport.explanation: 'By' a means of transport is בְּ: בְּאוֹטוֹבּוּס (by bus), בְּרַכֶּבֶת (by train), בְּמוֹנִית (by taxi), בִּמְכוֹנִית (by car). 'On foot' is בָּרֶגֶל. Ask the way with אֵיךְ מַגִּיעִים לְ…? ('how do you get to…?').
a1-transport.fact: On Shabbat most Israeli buses and trains don't run, from Friday afternoon until Saturday evening.

dialogue.en: How do you get to the central bus station?

a1-jobs.title: Jobs
a1-jobs.pattern: רוֹפֵא / רוֹפְאָה · מוֹרֶה / מוֹרָה · מְהַנְדֵּס / מְהַנְדֶּסֶת
a1-jobs.explanation: Job words have a masculine and a feminine form: רוֹפֵא / רוֹפְאָה (doctor), מוֹרֶה / מוֹרָה (teacher), מְהַנְדֵּס / מְהַנְדֶּסֶת (engineer), אָחוֹת (nurse). Say what someone does with no 'is': הִיא רוֹפְאָה ('she is a doctor'). Ask בְּמָה אַתָּה עוֹבֵד? ('what do you work in?').
a1-jobs.fact: Many Israelis serve in the army after school (usually 2–3 years) and only then go to university, so students are often older than in other countries.

dialogue.en: What do you do for work?

a1-compare.title: Bigger Than: יוֹתֵר … מִ
a1-compare.pattern: יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל מִ… (bigger than) · הֲכִי גָּדוֹל (the biggest)
a1-compare.explanation: To compare, put יוֹתֵר ('more') before the adjective and מִ ('from') before the thing compared: תֵּל אָבִיב יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה מֵחֵיפָה ('Tel Aviv is bigger than Haifa'). 'Less' is פָּחוֹת. 'The most' is הֲכִי: הֲכִי טוֹב ('the best'). Before ה, ח, ע, ר the prefix מִ becomes מֵ.
a1-compare.fact: הֲכִי טוֹב ('the best') is also an everyday reply meaning 'great, perfect'.

dialogue.native: מָה יוֹתֵר טָעִים, פִּיצָה אוֹ פָלָאפֶל?
